title: Ladies First
synopsis: Your small-town women's coalition has won a council seat. The seat is yours. The town is split. The first session is Monday and the agenda includes a budget you've been fighting for two years.

nodes.text: You win by 41 votes. Your mom cries. Your kid, eleven, is asleep on the couch. The coalition is in your living room making absurdly bad coffee.

choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Recognize.
You commit to “Save the thank-yous for Monday.” The story records the instinct as “Be presentable” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: The mayor, who endorsed your opponent, calls to congratulate you. He uses your first name without permission. He invites you to coffee. You realize he is, professionally, already negotiating.

choices.consequence: Politics is also rooms.
Set the boundary.

nodes.text: Your mother, who once ran for the same seat and lost twice, makes you sit on the porch with her. 'They will try to make you a kind of woman they can manage,' she says. 'Don't let them.'

choices.text: Ask her how she avoided that
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Listen—follows you into whatever comes next.

choices.text: Ask her what she thought she should have done differently
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Ask her what she thought she should have done differently” back. Different question shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: You sit at the council table for the first time. There are six of you. You are the only woman. The first item is, unbelievably, the budget you've been pushing for two years. The mayor calls you 'councilwoman' the way some men say 'ma'am.'

choices.consequence: Strike while warm.
The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Read—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: Wednesday night meeting at the church basement. Three new members. Two are nervous. One is, you can tell, already angling to be the next candidate. You realize you have to be a leader the coalition wants to follow.

choices.text: Make space for the ambitious one
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Make space for the ambitious one” back. Generosity shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Set firm expectations for the coalition
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Discipline—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: The vote is three to three. You sit with it for a long second. The deciding vote is, of course, an unexpected councilman who, you realize, is voting his conscience for the first time.

choices.consequence: Make him your ally.

choices.text: Thank him privately and protect him
choices.consequence: You commit to “Thank him privately and protect him.” The story records the instinct as “Strategic” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Your kid, eleven, asks you, with great seriousness, what your job is now. You think for a long minute. You realize the answer is, technically, 'I argue with men about how the town should work.'

choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Honest—follows you into whatever comes next.
There is no taking “Give her the kid-version” back. Gentle shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: The local paper writes an editorial about your first vote. It is, mostly, generous. It is, in one paragraph, condescending. You realize the editor is, separately, going to be your neighbor for a long time.

choices.text: Respond to the editorial in a letter
choices.consequence: You commit to “Respond to the editorial in a letter.” The story records the instinct as “On record” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Don't respond; let the work speak
choices.consequence: You commit to “Don't respond; let the work speak.” The story records the instinct as “Discipline” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Your first town hall as a councilmember. The room is louder than the council chamber. A man in the back yells about your funding decision. A woman near the front cries because of it.

choices.consequence: Calm the loudest.
Honor the quieter.

nodes.text: Three months in. A vote on whether to fund a new library or repair the old highway bridge. The county will subsidize either, not both. You can guess which option the men will pick.

choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Vision.
The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Pragmatism.

nodes.text: You and the unexpected councilman start meeting for breakfast. You don't agree on much. You agree on the budget for the food pantry. The breakfasts become, in their way, the actual government.

choices.consequence: There is no taking “Codify the alliance” back. Build shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.
You commit to “Keep it informal.” The story records the instinct as “Light” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: Two years pass. Your re-election campaign is, mercifully, less of a fight than the first. You win by 312 votes. The coalition has, in your absence, doubled.

choices.consequence: You commit to “Run for mayor next cycle.” The story records the instinct as “Aim up” and carries it forward.

choices.text: Stay on the council and build
choices.consequence: Stay in your strength.

nodes.text: Your daughter, thirteen now, sits in on a council meeting and watches you for two hours. Afterward she says, 'I want to do that.' You realize you have, accidentally, started a small generational thing.

choices.consequence: Pass the skill.

choices.text: Let her find her own version
choices.consequence: The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Independence.

nodes.text: You run for mayor. The town is, again, split. You win, again, narrowly. Your mother is in the audience at the swearing-in, in a dress she's owned since 1987. She doesn't cry. Her dress, she says, is too good.

choices.text: Make 'small town, big work' your platform
choices.consequence: “Make 'small town, big work' your platform” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Frame.
“Just do the work quietly” closes one possibility and opens another. The moment leaves a clear note behind: Substance.

nodes.text: The library opens, eventually. There is a small plaque with your name and three other names. Your daughter cuts the ribbon because you insisted. The whole coalition is in the front row. So is your mother.

choices.text: Use the library opening for the next campaign
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Build—follows you into whatever comes next.
Honor the win.

nodes.text: The first hundred days are paperwork, parking, ordinances. Glamorous it is not. You realize, slowly, that being mayor is mostly the work of returning calls. You return them.

choices.consequence: There is no taking “Keep returning every call personally” back. Old school shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.
You commit to “Hire a chief of staff.” The story records the instinct as “Scale yourself” and carries it forward.

nodes.text: You attend a county-wide conference of small-town officials. Half of them are women now. Five years ago, two of them were. You realize you have, accidentally, been part of a shift.

choices.text: Take the lead on a regional coalition
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Take the lead on a regional coalition” back. Bigger frame shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

choices.text: Stay focused on your own town
choices.consequence: There is no taking “Stay focused on your own town” back. Local shapes the silence before the next moment arrives.

nodes.text: Your first veto. The bill is, on balance, bad. The council member who proposed it is, separately, a friend's husband. You veto it. You call the friend the same night. The friendship survives. The friendship is, briefly, the work.

choices.consequence: Both at once.
Honest about cost.

nodes.text: You convene a coalition of nine towns. The first meeting is awkward. The second is, surprisingly, productive. By the third you are voted, against your wishes, the chair.

choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Take it.
The choice lands, and the scene changes around it. If it has a name, that name is Pass.

nodes.text: Eve of the re-election. The kitchen table, again, late. Your mother, in town for it, has made tea. Your daughter, fifteen, is writing your closing remarks for you. You realize the politics has, finally, become a family practice.

choices.text: Run again with the bigger 'small town' frame
choices.consequence: You let the choice stand. The path shifts almost imperceptibly, marked by one lasting impulse: Mayor again.

choices.text: Run again on quiet, careful substance
choices.consequence: The decision settles the question for now. Its verdict—Quiet—follows you into whatever comes next.

nodes.text: You serve two terms as mayor and shape, slowly, a town that looks like the town you wanted to grow up in. Your daughter, fifteen, runs for student council and wins. Your mother, in her late seventies, retires into proudly criticizing the new mayor.

You stay on the council. You build, quietly, slowly, decisively. People stop being surprised that a woman has the seat. Your kid grows up in a town that is, in small ways, kinder. That, you realize, was always the point.
